components.description: Motivation: legal mandate for fairness, causal fairness's advantages, and the unrealistic no-unobserved-confounding assumption.

nodes.name: Fairness legally mandated
nodes.description: Fairness of machine learning predictions is widely required by legal frameworks, notably in credit lending and law enforcement.

nodes.name: Causal fairness relates directly to legal terminology
nodes.description: Causal fairness leverages causal theory to ensure a sensitive attribute does not affect prediction outcomes, directly relating to legal terminology requiring outcome independence from sensitive attributes.

nodes.name: Existing causal fairness methods assume no unobserved confounding
nodes.description: Existing works on causally fair predictions commonly focus on settings with no unobserved confounding, assuming the causal structure is fully known.

nodes.name: No-confounding assumption is unrealistic
nodes.description: The assumption of no unobserved confounding is fairly strong and unrealistic in practice.

nodes.name: Unobserved confounding can violate causal fairness
nodes.description: Due to unobserved confounding, causal fairness may be violated, and predictions can cause harm as they may actually be unfair.

nodes.name: Prison sentence example illustrates the problem
nodes.description: In predicting prison sentences, unobserved confounders such as housing situation, family background, and birthplace can bias predictions if not accounted for, even when race is excluded and offense/crime history are controlled.

components.description: Research gap and positioning relative to related literature streams.

nodes.name: Sensitivity models exist for interventional effects only
nodes.description: Sensitivity models are common tools for partial identification under unobserved confounding, but they perform partial identification on interventional effects (level 2 of Pearl's ladder).

nodes.name: Causal fairness involves nested counterfactuals
nodes.description: Causal fairness involves nested counterfactual effects (level 3 of Pearl's ladder), which differ from the interventional effects that sensitivity models directly handle.

nodes.name: Sensitivity models not directly applicable
nodes.description: Because of the level mismatch between interventional effects and nested counterfactuals, it is not possible to directly apply existing sensitivity models to the causal fairness setting.

nodes.name: Kilbertus et al. only prior sensitivity-fairness work, but limited
nodes.description: The only prior work analyzing sensitivity of fairness to unobserved confounding (Kilbertus et al. 2019) focuses on counterfactual fairness, allows confounding only between covariates, and relies on restrictive non-linear additive noise model assumptions.

nodes.name: No work on causal fairness sensitivity to unobserved confounding
nodes.description: To the authors' knowledge, no work has analyzed the sensitivity of causal fairness specifically (as opposed to counterfactual fairness) to unobserved confounding.

nodes.name: Research gap established
nodes.description: The combination of the level mismatch, the narrow scope of prior sensitivity-fairness work, and the absence of causal-fairness-specific sensitivity analysis establishes the paper's research gap.

components.description: Standard Fairness Model setup with three sources of unobserved confounding and path-specific fairness effects.

nodes.name: Standard Fairness Model adopted
nodes.description: The paper adopts the Standard Fairness Model with data V = {A, Z, M, Y}: sensitive attribute A, observed confounders Z, mediators M, and outcome Y.

nodes.name: Three types of unobserved confounding modeled
nodes.description: The setup uniquely allows three types of unobserved confounding: direct (U_DE, between A and Y), indirect (U_IE, between A and M), and spurious (U_SE, between A and Z).

nodes.name: Path-specific effects defined
nodes.description: Path-specific causal fairness is defined via three effects: counterfactual direct effect (Ctf-DE) for A→Y, indirect effect (Ctf-IE) for A→M→Y, and spurious effect (Ctf-SE) for Z→A.

nodes.name: DE measures direct discrimination
nodes.description: Ctf-DE measures direct discrimination based on the sensitive attribute.

nodes.name: IE and SE measure indirect discrimination
nodes.description: Ctf-IE and Ctf-SE together measure indirect discrimination through factors related to the sensitive attribute, potentially acting as proxies.

nodes.name: Causal fairness achieved when effects near zero
nodes.description: Causal fairness is achieved when DE, IE, and SE are zero or close to zero, operationalized via user-defined thresholds.

components.description: From non-identifiability under confounding to the two-step bound-derivation workflow.

nodes.name: CF effects unidentifiable under unobserved confounding
nodes.description: Under unobserved confounding, the path-specific causal fairness effects (DE, IE, SE) are not identifiable from observational data, so naive estimates are biased.

nodes.name: Move from point to partial identification
nodes.description: As a remedy, the paper moves from point identification to partial identification, deriving upper and lower bounds for DE, IE, SE under a sensitivity model.

nodes.name: Step 1: counterfactual unnesting
nodes.description: Each CF is decomposed into identifiable parts and unnested (single-intervention) interventional effects, since sensitivity analysis operates on interventional (level-2) effects while CF involves nested (level-3) counterfactuals.

nodes.name: Step 2: sensitivity-model bounding
nodes.description: The unnested interventional effects are then bounded using the GMSM sensitivity model, yielding upper and lower bounds for each CF.

nodes.name: GMSM chosen for generality
nodes.description: The generalized marginal sensitivity model (GMSM) is adopted because it handles discrete mediators and both discrete/continuous outcomes, and subsumes many existing sensitivity models (e.g., MSM) as special cases.

edges.note: cross-component link from C2: level mismatch necessitates unnesting

components.description: Lemma 1 (unnesting) and the resulting sharp, general bounds of Theorem 1.

nodes.name: Lemma 1: CF as function of unidentifiable effects plus identifiable term
nodes.description: Lemma 1 shows each CF can be written as a monotonically increasing function of a sum of unidentifiable single-intervention effects plus an identifiable term q.

nodes.name: Unidentifiable effects can be bounded by sensitivity analysis
nodes.description: The unidentifiable single-intervention effects in Lemma 1's decomposition are exactly the type of effect that causal sensitivity analysis can bound.

nodes.name: Identifiable term estimable from data
nodes.description: The identifiable term q in the decomposition can be directly estimated from observational data.

nodes.name: Theorem 1: explicit bounds derived
nodes.description: Using the unnested expressions, Theorem 1 derives explicit closed-form upper and lower bounds on DE, IE, and SE under the GMSM for binary sensitive attribute A and discrete Z.

nodes.name: Bounds are distribution/SCM agnostic
nodes.description: Theorem 1's bounds are independent of the distribution and dimensionality of unobserved confounders and specific SCM formulations, applying to discrete, categorical, and continuous outcomes.

nodes.name: Bounds are sharp (Remark 2)
nodes.description: The derived bounds are sharp/optimal, meaning the supremum/infimum equality in the bound definition holds exactly.

nodes.name: Wider intervals indicate greater sensitivity
nodes.description: The wider the interval between CF+ and CF-, the more sensitive the path-specific effect is to unobserved confounding, giving less confidence in unconfounded estimates.

components.description: From bounds to a robust fair-prediction training objective.

nodes.name: CF bounds used to limit worst-case unfairness
nodes.description: Since path-specific causal fairness is unidentifiable under confounding, the derived bounds CF+ and CF- are used to limit the worst-case (maximum deviation from zero) unfairness of the prediction model.

nodes.name: Predicted outcome substituted into bound formulas
nodes.description: To train the model, P±(y|z,m,a) in the bounds is replaced by the non-random predicted outcome f_θ(a,z,m), requiring only estimation of P±(m|z,a) via pre-trained density estimators.

nodes.name: Constrained optimization objective formulated
nodes.description: The training objective is formulated as minimizing prediction loss subject to worst-case fairness bound constraints |CF+_E|,|CF-_E| ≤ γ_CF for each CF in {DE, IE, SE}.

nodes.name: Augmented Lagrangian used to solve constrained problem
nodes.description: To solve the constrained optimization with gradient-based solvers, augmented Lagrangian optimization is used to convert it into a single loss function with an estimated Lagrange multiplier.

nodes.name: Algorithm 1 trains the robust fair predictor
nodes.description: Algorithm 1 iteratively computes upper/lower CF bounds via Theorem 1, updates the Lagrangian loss, and updates the predictor parameters, checking convergence on both prediction loss and fairness constraints.

components.description: Experimental design: absence of baselines and the three-model comparison used instead.

nodes.name: No existing baselines for this setting
nodes.description: Baselines for causal fairness under unobserved confounding are absent in prior literature.

nodes.name: Three comparison models defined instead
nodes.description: Because no baselines exist, the paper compares three models with identical network architecture: Standard (no fairness constraint), Fair naive (fairness assuming no unobserved confounding), and Fair robust (the proposed framework).

nodes.name: Fair naive expected to be miscalibrated under confounding
nodes.description: Fair naive considers causal fairness only under the assumption of no unobserved confounding, so it is expected to underestimate true unfairness when confounding is present.

nodes.name: Identical architecture isolates the learning objective
nodes.description: Because the three models share identical network architecture, any fairness improvement can be attributed specifically to the tailored learning objective rather than model capacity.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: bounds for CF under unobserved confounding
nodes.description: Bounds are derived for causal fairness metrics under different sources of unobserved confounding, serving as a refutation strategy for practitioners.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: robust neural fair-prediction framework
nodes.description: A novel neural framework is developed for learning fair predictions with worst-case guarantees on the extent of causal fairness violation due to unobserved confounding.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: empirical demonstration including real-world case study
nodes.description: The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated in experiments on synthetic and real-world data, including a real-world case study predicting prison sentences.

isolated_nodes.name: Framework generalizes to other fairness notions
isolated_nodes.description: Although the paper focuses on DE, IE, SE, the bound-derivation framework can also be employed for other fairness notions.

isolated_nodes.name: Framework valid for known and unknown Gamma_W
isolated_nodes.description: The framework applies not only when the sensitivity parameter is known but is also of practical value when it is unknown, via data-driven heuristics.
